notes: Where quantity is unconfirmed, qty=1 is assumed. Purchase price, source and date of arrival to be added later.

flags.title: Possible bottle variation
flags.text: Canon struggled with TCA contamination in the cellar's woodwork through the 1990s and rebuilt the cellars after Chanel bought the estate in 1996. Quality got back on track in the mid-to-late 2000s, so the 2000 vintage falls in the transition. Don't put it up alone at an important dinner.

storage.note: Cellar held at a steady 10°C. Safe for long-term storage, and slightly below the ideal band (12–14°C), so ageing runs a little slower — the far end of each drinking window can be taken as having more room than the figures show. Reds serve at 16–18°C, though, so take them out of the cellar 40–60 minutes before opening.

price_note: Prices target the Wine-Searcher worldwide average. Automated access is blocked by a CAPTCHA, so they are graded by how they were obtained. Confirmed means the figure was read directly off the Wine-Searcher page. Estimated means a median of actual retailer listings for the matching vintage, outliers removed. Unverified means it was never read off the page — all six have since been corroborated by a second vintage-pinned search and agree within a few per cent, so none is a repeat of the Château Canon error, where a snippet gave $603 against an actual $220 by scraping an all-vintage page. Worth knowing when reading the total: the worldwide average runs above US retail. Lynch-Bages averages $166 worldwide against a US listing median near $117, and Alter Ego $122 against $103. This is a replacement value across markets, not a US shelf price. PRICES.md lists what is still outstanding, worst first.
vintage_note: Vintage ratings describe the growing season in that region and year, not this particular bottle — a great estate makes good wine in a poor year and the reverse happens too. They are reputations gathered from general knowledge, not measurements, and where one is shaky the note says so.

wines.notes: 2018 is a top-tier Napa vintage. Good now, fine for another five years. Decant 2 hours.
wines.short: Top-tier 2018 Napa, good now and will keep
wines.display: Orin Swift Mercury Head Cabernet Sauvignon

profile.tasting: Ripe blackberry and cassis with a thick layer of mocha and vanilla oak over the top. The Orin Swift house style puts overripe fruit and high alcohol out front, so it competes on density rather than finesse. The acidity of the 2018 vintage carries that weight.
profile.story: Dave Phinney's cult-minded Napa label. Mercury Head is the signature cuvée, released with a real Mercury dime — the US ten-cent piece struck in 90% silver until 1945 — fixed to the label.

price.note: Median of 6 retailer listings, $105–175. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $164.
price.source: Median of 6 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: A long, even growing season and a large crop of high quality. One of Napa's best recent years, with more freshness than the hot vintages either side of it.

wines.notes: Hardys' top Cabernet. Still young. Another two or three years at least.
wines.short: Still young, another two or three years at least

profile.tasting: Cassis and graphite layered over eucalyptus and mint. This is the cool-climate end of Australian Cabernet, so it has more edge than Napa and a tighter weave of tannin. Right now that tannin is still closed.
profile.story: Hardys' flagship, named after founder Thomas Hardy and released only in the best years. The fruit comes from Coonawarra and Margaret River.

price.note: Median of 4 retailer listings, $72–101. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $97.
price.source: Median of 4 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: A cool, late season in both Coonawarra and Margaret River after a wet winter. Lower alcohol and firmer acid than the Australian norm, which suits a wine built to age.

wines.notes: The most casual, everyday bottle in the cellar. No reason to hold it. Drink it down first.
wines.short: Everyday bottle, best right now

profile.tasting: Ripe plum and black cherry, vanilla and sweet oak. The fruit is forward enough to read as sweetness and the tannin is soft. It is built for immediate satisfaction rather than complexity, so drinking it now is right.
profile.story: Made by the Austin Hope family in Paso Robles. Scores in the 90s and an accessible price made it sell explosively in the US.

price.note: Median of 5 retailer listings, $50–78. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $66.
price.source: Median of 5 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: The California smoke year. The damage was concentrated in Napa and Sonoma and Paso Robles picks earlier, so it was far less exposed — but 2020 is the one California vintage worth tasting before you commit it to a table.

wines.notes: 2005 is a legendary Bordeaux vintage. The window has only just opened. No hurry.
wines.short: Legendary 2005 vintage, the window is open but it hits its stride in the 2030s

profile.tasting: Cassis and cedar, wet earth and tobacco leaf. The firm tannic frame typical of Saint-Estèphe, with Calon Ségur's own elegance laid over it. 2005 is high in both acidity and tannin, so there is a long way left to go.
profile.story: The heart on the label comes from the eighteenth-century owner, the Marquis de Ségur, who said his heart was at Calon. A third growth, but a château that has long fetched second-growth prices.

price.note: Median of 8 retailer listings, $94–280. Low confidence. The WS snippet ($210) sat above the listings and was excluded.
price.source: Median of 8 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: One of the two benchmark modern Bordeaux vintages. A dry summer without heat spikes gave ripe fruit and unusually high tannin, which is why these are still closed twenty years on.

wines.notes: 2021 is a very strong Napa vintage. Opening it now would be a waste.
wines.short: Very strong 2021 Napa, a waste to open now
wines.display: Shafer One Point Five Cabernet Sauvignon

profile.tasting: Black fruit with liquorice and cocoa, and the velvet texture of Stags Leap. Shafer's hand has polished the tannin fine, but the concentration of 2021 keeps the fruit balled up for now.
profile.story: One Point Five means between the first generation and the second — the handover from John Shafer to his son Doug, written into the name. Sold to Shinsegae in 2022.

price.note: Median of 8 retailer listings, $97–150. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $140.
price.source: Median of 8 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: A small crop after drought, and no smoke — the vintage that restored confidence after 2020. Concentrated and firmly structured.

wines.notes: Decant 2 hours if opening now. Better after 2028.
wines.short: Decant 2 hours if opening now, better after 2028

profile.tasting: Cherry and dried herbs, leather and earth, with the black fruit the Cabernet brings layered over them. Sangiovese's high acidity and scratchy tannin are at the centre, which makes it unusually good with Italian food. 2020 is a well-balanced year.
profile.story: The 1971 first vintage gave up Chianti Classico status on purpose in order to blend in Cabernet, and became the wine the Super Tuscans started from.

price.note: Median of 12 retailer listings, $150–213. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $183.
price.source: Median of 12 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: A warm, early Tuscan year. Less consistent than 2019, but the successful wines are generous and open earlier.

wines.notes: Millennium vintage, 26 years old. Exactly at peak now.
wines.short: Millennium vintage at 26 years, right at peak

profile.tasting: The fresh fruit has receded and tertiary aromas take the front — cedar, leather, dried plum, mushroom. The tannin has fully resolved into silk and the acidity still holds it up. A textbook point in the ageing of Bordeaux.
profile.story: The 2000 millennium vintage succeeded evenly across Bordeaux, and 26 years on most of the classed growths have moved into their best window.

serve.decant: 1–2 hours (to get it off the sediment)

price.note: Median of 4 retailer listings, $173–280. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $226.
price.source: Median of 4 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: The millennium vintage, and it earned the hype. Ripe, complete and successful on both banks — one of the reference Bordeaux years.

wines.wine: Le Petit Mouton de Mouton Rothschild
wines.notes: 2013 is a weak Bordeaux vintage. No reason to wait any longer. Drink within two years.
wines.short: Weak vintage, no reason to wait
wines.display: Le Petit Mouton de Mouton Rothschild

profile.tasting: Cassis and pencil lead, with the hint of spice that marks Mouton. It has none of the grand vin's density but the Pauillac frame is clear. Bad weather at flowering and rain at harvest left 2013 short on concentration, so it opened early.
profile.story: The second wine of Mouton Rothschild. It has carried the current name since 1993.

price.note: Median of 5 retailer listings, $183–527. Low confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $258.
price.source: Median of 5 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: The weakest modern Bordeaux vintage. A cold wet spring wrecked flowering and rot at harvest finished the job; even first-growth estates made light, early wines. That is why this one has a short window.

wines.notes: An underrated vintage, but Palmer is exceptionally good in it. One of the best bottles in the cellar.
wines.short: Underrated vintage, but Palmer is exceptionally good

profile.style: Margaux with a high proportion of Merlot
profile.tasting: Violets and black fruit, and the aromatic flamboyance particular to Margaux. Palmer is the only third growth to use close to half Merlot, which gives it a round texture and a sensual nose. 2008 is an underrated vintage, but Palmer was exceptionally successful in it.
profile.story: A third growth in the 1855 classification, but rated in practice at second-growth level or above, and one of the leading châteaux of Margaux. It converted to biodynamics in 2014.

price.note: Median of 5 retailer listings, $217–319. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $340.
price.source: Median of 5 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: Rescued by a long dry autumn after a difficult summer. Classical and firm, never fashionable, and consistently underrated.

wines.notes: A second wine at 26 years. Late in its peak. Drink it with high priority.
wines.short: Second wine at 26 years, late in its peak

profile.tasting: Violets and red fruit, the fine-boned Margaux nose. At 26 years the tannin has completely unwound and dried flowers and earth have come up. Being a second wine, its window closes earlier than the grand vin's, so don't wait.
profile.story: The second wine of Château Margaux. It has existed since 1908 and is one of the oldest second wines in Bordeaux.

price.note: Median of 9 retailer listings, $172–450. Low confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $307.
price.source: Median of 9 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: The millennium vintage, and it earned the hype. Ripe, complete and successful on both banks — one of the reference Bordeaux years.

wines.notes: 2007 is one of the best vintages Opus One has made. In a perfect window now. Two bottles of the same vintage.
wines.short: One of the best Opus One vintages ever

profile.tasting: Cassis and blackcurrant layered with cedar, pencil lead and tobacco leaf. It sits where Napa fruit concentration meets Bordeaux restraint, and at 19 years the tannin has fully resolved into a smooth texture. 2007 is one of the great years in Opus One's history.
profile.story: Napa's first ultra-premium project, founded in 1979 as a joint venture between Robert Mondavi and Baron Philippe de Rothschild.

price.note: Median of 8 retailer listings, $395–1050. Low confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $545.
price.source: Median of 8 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: A near-ideal season — small crop, even ripening, wines with both depth and acidity. Regarded as one of Napa's finest of the decade.

wines.notes: Multi-vintage blend. Not for ageing. Drink it early. Two bottles — open one without ceremony and keep the other to compare against.
wines.short: Multi-vintage blend, not for ageing

profile.style: The entry point to Opus One
profile.tasting: Cassis and cedar, like an abridged version of the Opus One nose. Blending several vintages keeps variation low and leaves it open from the start. There is nothing to gain by keeping it, so open it whenever.
profile.story: Opus One's non-vintage second wine. It used to be sold only to visitors at the winery and is now distributed normally.

price.note: Median of 11 retailer listings, $169–250. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $201.
price.source: Median of 11 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: Non-vintage: blended across years from lots that did not go into the grand vin. There is no vintage to rate.

wines.notes: 30 years old. Good storage history or not, it is at the end of the window. Top priority to drink. Decant briefly (30 minutes), watch the sediment.
wines.short: 30 years old, end of the drinking window

profile.tasting: Dried plum and fig, leather, tobacco and forest floor. The fresh fruit has all but gone and tertiary aromas dominate. At 30 years it is fragile, and long contact with air will collapse it fast — open it briefly and drink it straight away.
profile.story: First made in 1985, it put Bolgheri on the world map alongside Sassicaia. 1996 is one of the vintages that fixed Ornellaia's early reputation.

serve.decant: Under 30 minutes (just to get it off the sediment)

price.source: Median of 4 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)
price.note: Median of 4 retailer listings, $250–548. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $256.

vintage_note.text: A cooler, more classical Tuscan year than the ripe vintages around it. Bolgheri fared better than Chianti, but this is one to drink rather than wait on.

wines.notes: The most expensive and highest-classified bottle in the cellar. A first growth at 30 years, at its classic peak. For a special occasion.
wines.short: First growth at 30 years, classic peak. For a special occasion

profile.tasting: Tobacco, cigar box and baked earth over a bed of cassis, with the smoke and mineral note that signs every Haut-Brion. It is the most distinctive nose among the Bordeaux first growths, and at 30 years it has reached complete harmony.
profile.story: The only château outside the Médoc to be ranked a first growth in 1855. It is counted as the oldest brand-name wine in Bordeaux.

price.note: Median of 6 retailer listings, $580–685. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $613.
price.source: Median of 6 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: A great Cabernet year on the Left Bank — cool and late, giving firm structure and long life. The Right Bank, where Merlot never fully ripened, got a very different 1996.

wines.notes: Silver Oak is built to be ready to drink on release. 30 years is the limit. Drink first.
wines.short: Early-drinking style plus 30 years of age
wines.display: Silver Oak Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon

profile.tasting: Coconut, dill and vanilla — the signature of the American oak ageing Silver Oak insists on, ahead of the fruit. After 30 years the fruit has most likely faded a long way, so adjust expectations before opening.
profile.story: A Napa winery known for releasing its wines already ready to drink. It is one of the few top-level producers to use American oak exclusively.

price.note: Median of 4 retailer listings, $148–200. High confidence. The WS snippet ($226) sat above the listings and was excluded.
price.source: Median of 4 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: An uneven year in Napa after a difficult flowering. Good rather than great, and at thirty years old there is nothing to gain by waiting.

wines.notes: 2019 is an all-time Sassicaia vintage. Opening it now is a loss. Hold to 2030 at the least.
wines.short: All-time vintage, a loss to open now

profile.tasting: Cabernet cassis and cedar layered with Mediterranean herbs and salty minerality. Sassicaia is lighter and higher-toned than Bordeaux, but the 2019 structure is unusually firm and it is closed right now. After 2030 is where it really comes into its own.
profile.story: First commercial release in 1968. It is the only wine in Italy with a DOC of its own (Bolgheri Sassicaia).

price.note: Median of 12 retailer listings, $250–460. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $322.
price.source: Median of 12 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: An excellent Tuscan vintage — a cool August and warm September gave ripeness with the acidity intact. Rated among the best of the decade in Bolgheri.

wines.notes: Open this first of the three DPs. Fully mature now.
wines.short: Open this first of the three DPs

profile.tasting: Brioche and hazelnut, baked apple, and the iodine and smoke that mark DP. At 16 years the bead has settled fine and the texture has turned creamy. It is the most developed of the three DPs, so open it first.
profile.story: Dom Pérignon is a vintage-only cuvée, declared just in the good years. 2010 was a difficult year, but selection held the wine together.

price.note: Median of 5 retailer listings, $270–320. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $352.
price.source: Median of 5 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: A hard year. Rot pressure in Pinot Noir forced severe selection and several houses declined to declare; those that did leaned on Chardonnay. A declared 2010 says more about the house's sorting than about the season.

wines.notes: A high-acid, tense vintage. Good now and good for longer.
wines.short: High acidity and tension, good now and good for longer

profile.tasting: Citrus, white flowers and flint. 2013 was cool and ripened late, so the acidity is high and the outline sharp. Good now, but with more time the texture will fill out.
profile.story: Dom Pérignon keeps evolving in the cellar after release, and high-acid vintages like this one last the longest.

price.note: Median of 12 retailer listings, $191–400. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $312.
price.source: Median of 12 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: A late, cool season picked into October. High acidity and slow development — built for long ageing rather than early charm.

wines.notes: The youngest DP. Hold.
wines.short: The youngest DP

profile.tasting: Citrus and white fruit, at a stage where the yeasty notes have not fully come up yet. The potential is clear, but opening it now means missing the complexity that is the point of DP. Better after 2028.
profile.story: The youngest of the three DPs in the cellar. Kept alongside the 2010 and the 2013 it makes an excellent vertical.

price.note: Median of 9 retailer listings, $240–308. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $277.
price.source: Median of 9 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: Rain and rot at harvest made 2017 one of the more difficult recent years and few prestige cuvées were declared. Treat a declared 2017 as a selection exercise.

wines.wine: Libera Me Brut — Blanc de Noirs
wines.notes: Identity confirmed. A small family producer founded in 2008, based at Colombé-le-Sec in the Aube (Côte des Bar). The wine is made in outbuildings of the Clairvaux abbey that have stood in the village since 1194 — the vaulted abbey cellar on the label and the name 'Libera Me' (from the Requiem liturgy) both come from that. Clay-limestone soils, two thirds Pinot Noir plus Chardonnay. Libera Me is the Pinot Noir-based Blanc de Noirs. Gold medals at the Lyon international wine competition (2013, 2019). Non-vintage, so not one to keep — drink within three years. There is a separate Brut Nature version under the same name, but this bottle is the Brut.
wines.short: Non-vintage grower Champagne, nothing to gain by keeping it
wines.display: Monial Libera Me Brut (Blanc de Noirs)

profile.tasting: Red apple and ripe pear, with the flesh and round texture of a Blanc de Noirs. The warm character of the Aube (Côte des Bar) comes through directly. Instead of the precision of a big house, the appeal is how direct the fruit is.
profile.story: A family producer founded in 2008. They work in outbuildings of the Clairvaux abbey that have stood at Colombé-le-Sec since 1194, and 'Libera Me' is taken from the Requiem liturgy.

price.note: Median of 4 retailer listings, $24–36. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $19.
price.source: Median of 4 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: Non-vintage, blended across years in the Côte des Bar. For a grower working at this scale the blend is the house's own signature rather than a statement about a particular season.

wines.notes: Cristal shows what it is worth with another five to ten years after release. The longest keeper among the cellar's Champagnes.
wines.short: The longest keeper among the cellar's Champagnes

profile.tasting: Lemon peel and white flowers, with the minerality still wound tight. Cristal needs five to ten years past release before its silk texture and nutty flavours open up. Open it now and you see less than half of what it has.
profile.story: A cuvée made in 1876 for Tsar Alexander II of Russia; the name comes from the clear crystal bottle, used because of fears of assassination.

price.note: Median of 15 retailer listings, $270–460. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $347.
price.source: Median of 15 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: Frost, mildew and a miserable spring cut the crop hard before a hot dry summer rescued what survived. Better in the glass than the growing season deserved.

wines.notes: A prestige cuvée at 20 years. Good now.
wines.short: Prestige cuvée at 20 years

profile.tasting: Toasted brioche and honey, dried apricot. At 20 years a fine oxidative note has settled over it and the bubbles have softened. Less known than Krug or DP, but complete enough.
profile.story: Pommery's prestige cuvée, named after Madame Louise Pommery, who popularised brut Champagne in the nineteenth century.

price.note: Median of 4 retailer listings, $241–330. High confidence.
price.source: Median of 4 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: A warm, generous year. Rich and forward rather than tense, so it has been drinking well for some time already.

wines.notes: Label checked (2022, white, 12.5%). The historic Domaine Charles Noëllat was sold to Leroy in 1988 and ceased to exist, but the name survives as a négociant brand → not a domaine wine but a négociant-bottled village-level wine. 2022 was a hot vintage, so acidity is low and the fruit full. Not suitable for keeping, drink by 2027. 12–13°C, white Burgundy glass.
wines.short: Négociant village level plus a low-acid vintage, not for keeping

profile.tasting: Yellow apple and citrus, light hazelnut and butter. 2022 was a hot year, so acidity is low and the fruit full, at the cost of tension. It is négociant village level, so set expectations at an easy everyday white Burgundy.
profile.story: Domaine Charles Noëllat disappeared when it was sold to Leroy in 1988, but the name stayed on as a négociant brand and is still in use. This bottle is that brand's bottling.

price.note: Median of 2 retailer listings, $116–136. Medium confidence.
price.source: Median of 2 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: A hot, dry year that made better wine than the weather suggested. The whites came in ripe and generous but short on acidity, so 2022 white Burgundy is open early and not a vintage to hold — which is the main thing to know about this bottle.

wines.notes: 2002 is one of the century's best Champagne vintages. Krug 2002 is legendary. Another 20 years from here. The highlight of the cellar.
wines.short: One of the century's best Champagne vintages. The highlight of the cellar

profile.tasting: Toasted nuts and brioche, marmalade and coffee. Krug's oxidative complexity plus the concentration of 2002 makes the density overwhelming. 24 years on it is still climbing, and it has another 20 years in it.
profile.story: Krug does the first fermentation of every cuvée in small oak casks. 2002 is reckoned the best Champagne vintage of the century, and Krug 2002 is called a legend even within it.

serve.decant: None (take it out an hour ahead and the nose opens up more)

price.note: Median of 10 retailer listings, $485–918. High confidence. Cross-checked against the WS snippet of $724.
price.source: Median of 10 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: One of the benchmark modern Champagne vintages, ripe and structured at once. Still the reference point everything else is measured against.

wines.notes: Antinori's top cuvée, above Tignanello. 2021 is rated a top-tier Tuscan vintage. The structure and tannin are firm, so hold to 2029 at the least; 2032–2045 is the core window. One of the longest keepers in the cellar.
wines.short: Core window 2032–2045

profile.tasting: Cassis and blackberry, cedar and balsamic. Unlike Tignanello, Cabernet leads here, which brings it close to Bordeaux, but the acidity and bitter edge from the Sangiovese keep the Italian identity. The 2021 structure is extremely firm.
profile.story: First vintage 1978. It comes from the best parcels within the Tignanello vineyard and is made only in good years.

price.note: Median of 7 retailer listings, $359–565. High confidence.
price.source: Median of 7 actual retailer listings, triangulated (USD/750ml)

vintage_note.text: A cool, dry season with a small crop, giving firm structure and depth. Rated at the top of the decade in Tuscany.

wines.notes: Owned by Castéja, distributed exclusively by Borie-Manoux, château-bottled. A small mid-tier Pomerol estate, Merlot-led. 1996 favoured the Left Bank (Médoc, Cabernet) and was a difficult vintage for Right Bank Merlot → not built for long ageing. At 30 years it is at the end of the drinking window, so drink it first. Stand it upright for 48 hours before opening, ease the cork out carefully with an Ah-So (two-pronged) puller, and decant briefly (20–30 minutes) or pour straight from the bottle. 16–17°C.
wines.short: 30 years old plus a vintage that hurt the Right Bank, no ageing left

profile.tasting: Dried plum and fig, earth and mushroom, and the round texture Merlot gives. At 30 years the fruit will have faded a long way and tertiary aromas dominate. 1996 favoured the Left Bank, so don't expect much of a Right Bank wine.
profile.story: A small Pomerol property owned by the Castéja family. Pomerol has no official classification, so a château's own reputation is all there is.

serve.decant: 30 minutes (just to get it off the sediment)

price.source: Confirmed by the owner directly on the Wine-Searcher screen (2026-09)
price.verified: Confirmed by the owner directly on the Wine-Searcher screen (2026-09)

vintage_note.text: 1996 was a Left Bank year. On the Right Bank, Merlot struggled to ripen in a cool late season, so Pomerol 1996 is the weaker half of a great vintage.

wines.short: Strong 2019 vintage, drinkable now but it hits its stride after 2029
wines.notes: Palmer's second wine, but not a 'little Palmer' — a cuvée made in a separate style, with the fruit out front and quicker to approach. 2019 is one of the best recent Bordeaux vintages, so the structure is firm. Decant 2 hours if opening now. Put it next to #9, Palmer 2008, and the grand vin / Alter Ego contrast is obvious.

profile.tasting: Red fruit and violets, fresh spice. It is Palmer's second wine but it is not a scaled-down grand vin; it is made as a separate style that leads with fruit. The concentration of 2019 means power comes first for now.
profile.story: The cuvée Palmer launched in 2002 after rethinking what a second wine is. As the name 'alter ego' says, a different character was the intention.

serve.decant: 2 hours (2029 onwards is the sweet spot)

price.note: Re-checked: the Wine-Searcher average still reads $122. US retailer listings run $92–150 (median about $103).
price.source: Wine-Searcher average quoted in search results, corroborated by a second vintage-pinned search — not read off the page itself

vintage_note.text: Hot but well balanced, with the drought relieved at the right moments. Ripe and fresh at once, and among the strongest recent Bordeaux vintages.

wines.short: Middling vintage so it opened early, a good window now
wines.notes: A Pauillac fifth growth known as 'the poor man's Mouton'. 2011 is a middling vintage caught between 2009 and 2010; it matured quickly and is good to approach now. 15 years old, decant 1–1.5 hours. Good with sirloin and lamb chops.

profile.tasting: Cassis and pencil lead, cedar and tobacco leaf — the textbook Pauillac nose. Lynch-Bages sits at the fuller-fruited end of that. 2011 is a middling vintage that matured quickly, so it is good to approach now.
profile.story: A fifth growth known as 'the poor man's Mouton'. It has long been rated well above its classification.

price.note: Re-checked against a vintage-pinned search: the Wine-Searcher average still reads $166. US retailer listings run $110–215 (median about $117), so the worldwide average sits well above what a US buyer pays.
price.source: Wine-Searcher average quoted in search results, corroborated by a second vintage-pinned search — not read off the page itself

vintage_note.text: Caught between the twin greats of 2009 and 2010. An erratic, uneven season gave lighter, earlier-maturing wines. Fine now, not one to wait on.

wines.short: Sauvignon Blanc, freshness is the whole point. Drink within a year
wines.notes: Label correction: Fines Caillions → Domaine des Fines Caillottes. The flint and citrus come from the limestone gravel (caillottes) soils. 2024 is very young = this is the peak. Nothing to gain by keeping it, so drink within a year. 8–10°C, with oysters, goat cheese or salad.
wines.display: Jean Pabiot Domaine des Fines Caillottes

profile.tasting: Grapefruit and gooseberry, flint and chalky minerality. The sharp acidity of Loire Sauvignon is the centre of it and no oak is used. The 2024 has only just come out, so this is exactly its peak.
profile.story: The Pabiot family named their estate Domaine des Fines Caillottes to tell themselves apart from the six other Pabiots in Pouilly. Caillottes are the small limestone stones of these soils, and they are where the mineral edge of Pouilly-Fumé comes from. The 2024 is 100% Sauvignon Blanc, fermented with wild yeasts and held several months on the lees; it took a gold medal at the Concours Général Agricole in Paris.

price.note: Re-checked: the Wine-Searcher average reads $32, against the $31 recorded. UK retail is £21.95.

vintage_note.text: A miserable French vintage — a wet spring, heavy mildew pressure and a small crop across the Loire. Drink it young for whatever freshness it has.

wines.short: At peak, but watch for bottle variation — see below
wines.notes: One thing to watch: Canon had serious trouble with TCA (cork taint) contamination in the cellar's woodwork through the 1990s, and after Chanel bought the estate in 1996 the cellars were stripped out and rebuilt wholesale. Quality only clearly got back on track from the mid-to-late 2000s, so the 2000 vintage falls in the transition. The vintage itself is excellent and a good bottle is very good right now, but allow for variation from bottle to bottle. Better opened somewhere there is a backup bottle than put up alone at an important dinner. Decant 1 hour.

profile.tasting: Red fruit and violets, with the straight minerality that comes off limestone. Canon is at the finesse-and-tension end of Saint-Émilion rather than the powerful end. For this vintage, though, read the caution below.
profile.story: A Saint-Émilion Premier Grand Cru Classé B, bought by Chanel in 1996. TCA contamination in the cellars was severe at the time of the purchase, so they were stripped out and rebuilt, and quality only clearly got back on track from the mid-to-late 2000s.

price.source: Confirmed by the owner directly on the Wine-Searcher screen (2026-09)
price.verified: Confirmed by the owner directly on the Wine-Searcher screen (2026-09)

vintage_note.text: 2000 was a great Bordeaux vintage on both banks. The caveat here is the estate rather than the year: Canon was still rebuilding from the TCA contamination and did not hit its stride until the mid-2000s.

wines.short: A half bottle, so it ages fast; good now
wines.notes: 375ml half bottle (confirmed). A Barsac first growth, the highest-acid and leanest style in Sauternes. A half bottle oxidises nearly twice as fast as a 750ml, so it ages quicker → at 24 years it is fully developed and there is no reason to wait. 8–10°C, with foie gras, blue cheese or tarte tatin. Keeps a week in the fridge once opened.

profile.tasting: Apricot and orange marmalade and honey, with the high Barsac acidity cutting through like a knife. It is the lightest, freshest style in Sauternes, so the sweetness does not sit heavy. At 375ml it ages fast, and now is good.
profile.story: A Barsac first growth. Barsac sits inside the Sauternes AOC but its soils are more limestone, which gives sweet wines with higher acidity and a sharper outline.

price.note: Still nothing vintage-specific. Coutet half-bottles are listed across many vintages but not 2002, so this figure remains the weakest in the cellar.
price.source: Wine-Searcher average quoted in search results, corroborated by a second vintage-pinned search — not read off the page itself

vintage_note.text: A decent botrytis year in Barsac without the concentration of 2001, the vintage of that era. Balanced and lighter, which suits a half-bottle that has aged faster.

wines.short: 45 years old but within normal range. The longest-lived bottle in the cellar
wines.notes: Moulin Touchais is known for ageing its wines at the estate for at least ten years before release, so 45 years is nothing out of the ordinary by this house's standard. The strong acidity of Chenin Blanc makes it extremely long-lived even among sweet wines — another 20 years is possible. The bottle with the most time in hand in the cellar. Honey, quince and caramel, with acidity holding the structure up. 10–12°C, no decanting. On its own or with a fruit tart.

profile.tasting: Honey and quince, dried apricot and caramel, with the strong acidity of Chenin Blanc running straight through. 45 years on it is still within normal range by this house's standard, and the acidity gives it another 20 years. The bottle with the most time in hand in the cellar.
profile.story: Moulin Touchais is known for keeping its wines in the cellar at least ten years after harvest before release. It is one of the few producers whose 40-year-old vintages, like this 1981, are still normally available on the market.

price.note: Corroborated by real listings rather than a quoted average: $47.95 and $57.00 for the 1981, median about $52. A third listing at $11.99 is implausible for a forty-five-year-old sweet Loire and was discarded.
price.source: Wine-Searcher average quoted in search results, corroborated by a second vintage-pinned search — not read off the page itself

vintage_note.text: Not a celebrated Loire year, and I could not verify much about 1981 in the Layon specifically. Moulin Touchais holds everything for decades before release, which flattens the difference between vintages more than most producers.

wines.wine: Dama de Naveran Extra Brut Cava
wines.display: Naveran Dama de Naveran Extra Brut Cava
wines.short: Three bottles left. The everyday pour.
wines.notes: Three left of the original four, so this is still the one that gets opened without a reason. Drink over the next two years.

profile.tasting: Green apple and lemon peel over a fine, insistent bead, with a light bready note from two years on the lees. The Chardonnay carries it and the Parellada keeps the finish lifted; the low dosage means it lands dry and clean rather than soft.
profile.story: Caves Naveran is a family estate in Torrelavit, in the Alt Penedès, working its own organically farmed fruit rather than bought-in grapes — unusual for Cava, where scale usually wins. Dama is 85% Chardonnay with 15% Parellada, aged 18 to 24 months on the lees.

price.source: Median of US retailer listings seen directly (USD/750ml)
price.note: Retailers seen at $29.99 (Flatiron SF) and $34.00 (Solano Cellars), with around $30 quoted as the average. Not read off a Wine-Searcher page.

vintage_note.text: A hot, dry drought year in Catalonia with a small crop. Cava held its acidity better than still wine did, but 2022 was hard work.

wines.short: Classic Penedès trio, Xarel·lo-led.
wines.notes: Bohigas' most widely distributed cuvée. The window is soft: this is non-vintage, so without a disgorgement date there is nothing to anchor it to — read it as roughly four years from a 2024 purchase.

profile.tasting: The classic Penedès signature, Xarel·lo-led: quince, almond skin and a faintly bitter herbal edge that keeps it savoury. Two years on the lees give it texture rather than fruit. Less forward than Chardonnay-led Cava, and better at the table for it.
profile.story: Caves Bohigas, also known as Fermí Bohigas, has been bottling since 1870 and works 35 hectares of estate vineyards at Òdena, in the higher inland part of Penedès where cooler nights hold acidity. The Brut Reserva is 55% Xarel·lo, 30% Macabeo and 15% Parellada, aged a minimum of 24 months.

price.source: US retailer listings seen directly (USD/750ml)
price.note: Listings seen from $13.99 to $18.99, with $19 quoted as the ex-tax average. Not read off a Wine-Searcher page.

vintage_note.text: Non-vintage. A Reserva Cava is blended across years and held a minimum of two years on the lees, so the house style matters more here than any one season — which is also why the drinking window on this bottle is soft.

wines.short: Magnum. The only large format in the cellar.
wines.notes: Magnum, so it ages more slowly than the 750ml and holds a year or two longer. A large format needs a table of six or more — plan it.

profile.tasting: Passionfruit, grapefruit and cut grass over a taut line of acidity, with a saline finish that keeps it from turning sweet-fruited. The magnum format slows oxidation, so this shows a shade more restraint than the 750ml of the same vintage.
profile.story: The wine that made Marlborough famous in 1985 and effectively created the international market for New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc. Now owned by LVMH, still the reference point for the style.

price.source: Wine-Searcher average quoted in search results, corroborated by a second vintage-pinned search — not read off the page itself
price.note: Re-checked: the Wine-Searcher average for the 750ml reads $33, up from the $32 recorded. No listing found for the magnum itself, so it is still valued at twice the 750ml price.

vintage_note.text: Cyclone Gabrielle hit New Zealand in February 2023 but spared Marlborough the worst of it. A large, healthy harvest, less concentrated than 2022.
